title: CAN YOU BE DEPRESSED AND STILL TRUST JESUS?
paragraphs:
CAN YOU BE DEPRESSED AND STILL TRUST JESUS?
What if the darkness in your mind is not proof that you have lost your faith—but the very place where you are discovering what it actually means to need a Savior?
There are Christians reading this who know exactly how to look okay.
You know when to smile.
You know when to say, “God is good.”
You know which Bible verse to post.
You know how to worship while people are watching.
And maybe nobody knows that when the room becomes quiet, something inside you collapses.
You love Jesus.
But you are tired.
You believe God is real.
But some mornings you do not want to get out of bed.
You know the promises.
But your emotions seem incapable of feeling them.
And somewhere along the way, perhaps somebody gave you another burden to carry.
“If you really trusted God, you wouldn’t feel like this.”
So now you are carrying two pains.
The darkness itself...
and the shame of wondering whether the darkness means you are disappointing Jesus.
Please hear this carefully:
The Bible does not teach that genuine faith means never experiencing profound emotional anguish.
In fact, Scripture is far more emotionally honest than many Christians allow themselves to be.
Listen to the psalmist:
מַה־תִּשְׁתּוֹחֲחִי נַפְשִׁי וַתֶּהֱמִי עָלָי הוֹחִילִי לֵאלֹהִים
“Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me? Hope in God...” — Psalm 42:5
Notice what happens here.
The psalmist does not pretend his soul is fine.
The Hebrew says, “מַה־תִּשְׁתּוֹחֲחִי... נַפְשִׁי” — “Why are you cast down, my soul?”
נַפְשִׁי, nafshi, means “my soul,” “my life,” “my self.”
And then comes the command:
הוֹחִילִי לֵאלֹהִים
Hochili l’Elohim.
“Hope in God.”
That is breathtaking.
His soul is cast down...
and he tells that same soul to hope in God.
The anguish and the faith are present in the same person.
That matters.
Because perhaps you have been measuring faith by how emotionally strong you feel when Scripture sometimes shows faith as what you cling to precisely when you do not feel strong.
Faith is not always shouting from a mountaintop.
Sometimes faith is whispering the name “Jesus” from the floor.
Sometimes faith is opening your Bible with trembling hands.
Sometimes faith is praying when the only prayer you can produce is:
“Lord, help me.”
Sometimes faith is simply refusing to walk away from Christ while everything inside you is screaming that you cannot continue.
And if you think real servants of God never reached places like that, listen to Paul.
This is an apostle.
A missionary.
A preacher.
A man who suffered for Christ and proclaimed the risen Jesus across the ancient world.
Yet Paul wrote:
“Οὐ γὰρ θέλομεν ὑμᾶς ἀγνοεῖν... ὥστε ἐξαπορηθῆναι ἡμᾶς καὶ τοῦ ζῆν.”
He explains that the affliction he and his companions experienced was so overwhelming that they “despaired even of life.” — 2 Corinthians 1:8.
The Greek word is devastating:
ἐξαπορηθῆναι — exaporēthēnai.
To despair. To be utterly at a loss.
Paul did not write, “Nothing bothered me because I had enough faith.”
He said they were burdened beyond their strength and despaired even of life.
And then Paul tells us where that terrible experience drove them.
Not away from God.
Deeper into dependence upon God.
He continues by explaining that they felt they had received the sentence of death so that they would not rely upon themselves, “but on God who raises the dead” (2 Corinthians 1:9).
There it is.
Christian faith does not always mean:
“I feel strong because God is with me.”
Sometimes it means:
“I have discovered that I am not strong enough, so my entire weight is falling upon the God who raises the dead.”
Maybe that is where you are.
You are not asking Jesus to make you impressive anymore.
You are asking Him to keep you alive inside.
And Scripture knows that territory.
Look at Elijah.
Be careful here: the Bible does not give Elijah a modern psychiatric diagnosis, so we should not pretend Scripture says something it does not say.
But 1 Kings 19 unquestionably describes a servant of God experiencing extraordinary fear, exhaustion, isolation and despair.
This is the same Elijah who had just stood at Mount Carmel.
Fire fell.
God answered.
The prophets of Baal were defeated.
You might expect Elijah to become spiritually untouchable after witnessing something like that.
Instead, Jezebel threatens his life.
And Elijah runs.
Eventually he sits beneath a broom tree.
Alone.
Exhausted.
And he says:
“It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life...” — 1 Kings 19:4.
Read that again.
A prophet who had seen fire fall from heaven reached a moment when he did not want to continue living.
Yesterday’s spiritual victory did not make him immune to tomorrow’s emotional collapse.
And look at what God does next.
God does not stand over Elijah screaming:
“Where is your faith?”
God lets him sleep.
God provides food.
God provides water.
Elijah sleeps again.
God feeds him again.
Only afterward does the journey continue.
There is something profoundly tender about this scene.
The God who could send fire from heaven also cared about an exhausted man needing food and sleep.
Sometimes we make spirituality so abstract that we forget God created bodies too.
You are not merely a floating soul.
You are an embodied human being.
Sleep matters.
Food matters.
Trauma matters.
Grief matters.
Relationships matter.
Your nervous system is not an enemy of Christianity.
And receiving appropriate help is not automatically evidence that you have abandoned God.
If you broke your leg, seeking medical care would not necessarily mean you had stopped trusting Jesus.
Likewise, seeking qualified help for serious mental or emotional suffering does not automatically mean you have replaced Jesus.
Christ remains Lord.
Christ remains Savior.
Christ remains our ultimate hope.
But the Lord routinely works through means.
He works through pastors.
Friends.
Family.
Doctors.
Counselors.
Medicine.
Rest.
Community.
Prayer.
Scripture.
And sometimes through the person who notices you have become unusually quiet and refuses to leave you alone.
Please do not turn suffering into a competition between prayer and appropriate care.
Pray.
And ask for help.
Read Scripture.
And tell somebody the truth.
Seek Christ.
And if you are experiencing persistent depression, speak with an appropriately qualified healthcare professional.
You do not glorify God by hiding dangerous suffering simply because you are afraid someone will question your faith.
There is another Man in Scripture we must talk about.
Jesus.
No, Jesus was not sinful.
No, we should not casually impose modern diagnoses upon Him.
But the Son of God was not emotionally numb.
At Lazarus’ tomb:
“Jesus wept.” — John 11:35.
And in Gethsemane, Jesus said:
“Περίλυπός ἐστιν ἡ ψυχή μου ἕως θανάτου.”
“My soul is deeply sorrowful, even to death.” — Matthew 26:38.
Περίλυπος — perilypos.
Deeply grieved.
Overwhelmed with sorrow.
The sinless Son of God experienced crushing sorrow without that sorrow making Him sinful.
Jesus knows what tears taste like.
He knows betrayal.
He knows abandonment.
He knows anguish.
He knows what it means to cry out.
Christianity does not give you a Savior standing far away from human suffering.
It gives you Jesus Christ.
God the Son who entered our suffering.
The Word became flesh.
He was rejected.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified.
And from the cross came that haunting cry:
“My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”
Jesus was invoking Psalm 22—the prayer of the righteous sufferer.
And here is where Christianity refuses to end the story where despair wants to end it.
The cross was not the last page.
The tomb was not the last page.
Friday was not the last page.
Jesus rose.
That changes everything.
Christian hope is not the claim that believers never enter darkness.
Christian hope is that darkness does not get the final word.
Depression may speak.
Grief may speak.
Trauma may speak.
Your past may speak.
Your exhaustion may speak.
Your own mind may sometimes accuse you.
But none of them gets to be your Savior.
Jesus does.
And perhaps the deepest question is not merely, “Can a Christian be depressed?”
Perhaps it is:
“Will Jesus still receive me when I am?”
Look at Him.
The Jesus who welcomed failures.
The Jesus who touched lepers.
The Jesus who restored Peter after Peter publicly denied Him.
The Jesus who ate with sinners.
The Jesus who carried a cross for guilty people.
The Jesus who prayed for His executioners.
The Jesus who told a dying criminal beside Him that paradise was coming.
Do you really think your tears frighten Him?
Do you think your exhausted prayers surprise Him?
Do you think He discovered your weakness this morning?
He already knew.
And still He went to the cross.
That is grace.
Grace is not God discovering that you are stronger than you thought.
Grace is discovering that Christ is sufficient when you finally admit you are not.
Maybe you have sins that need repentance.
Bring them into the light.
Maybe depression has become tangled together with isolation, bitterness, destructive habits, addiction, shame or secret sin.
Do not hide those things behind a diagnosis.
Repent where repentance is needed.
But do not call every symptom of suffering a sin either.
We need enough biblical wisdom to distinguish guilt from grief.
Both need Jesus.
But not in exactly the same way.
Sin needs forgiveness.
Wounds need healing.
Falsehood needs truth.
Isolation needs community.
Exhaustion may need rest.
Illness may need treatment.
And every human heart ultimately needs reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
The Gospel is bigger than “cheer up.”
The Gospel says something infinitely stronger.
You were separated from God by sin, and you could not rescue yourself.
Christ came for sinners.
He lived the righteousness we failed to live.
He died for sins.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith receives forgiveness and life.
Your deepest hope is therefore not that tomorrow morning you will suddenly feel amazing.
Your deepest hope has a name.
Jesus.
Feelings rise.
Feelings fall.
Christ remains.
There will be mornings when you feel the truth.
There may be mornings when you have to believe the truth while feeling almost none of its comfort.
Jesus remains Lord in both mornings.
So perhaps trust looks different tonight.
Maybe trust means calling somebody and saying:
“I’m not okay.”
Maybe trust means making the appointment you have been postponing.
Maybe trust means asking your church family for prayer.
Maybe trust means getting out of isolation.
Maybe trust means eating something, sleeping, stepping outside and allowing your body to breathe.
Maybe trust means opening Psalm 42 and borrowing somebody else’s words because you cannot find your own.
Maybe trust means whispering:
“Jesus, I cannot carry myself anymore.”
Good.
Christianity never required you to save yourself.
There is already a Savior.
And His name is Jesus Christ.

If thoughts of suicide or self-harm are part of what you are experiencing, please do not treat that as a private spiritual test you have to survive alone. Tell someone you trust immediately and contact emergency services or a crisis service where you live. Stay with another person and put distance between yourself and anything you could use to hurt yourself. Asking for immediate help is not spiritual failure. Your life matters, and you should not face that moment alone.
And to the Christian reading this who is not depressed...
please remember this article when somebody you love is.
Do not hand them a cliché and disappear.
Sit down.
Listen.
Bring food.
Call tomorrow.
Pray with them.
Help them find qualified care when needed.
Walk with them.
Bear one another’s burdens.
Sometimes the most Christlike thing you can do is remain beside someone long enough for them to realize their suffering did not make them untouchable.
And maybe that is why this article needs to leave your screen.
Someone on your Facebook friends list may be smiling publicly and collapsing privately.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God—it does not.
We are saved by grace, not social-media engagement.
Send it privately to the person whose silence has been worrying you.
Because there may come a night when you need these truths yourself.
If you are exhausted but still holding onto Christ, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
Someone reading underneath this article may desperately need evidence that another believer has walked through a dark valley and discovered that Christ was still there.

If you want to glorify God through supporting Gospel work, let that support flow from grace, not guilt. Pray. Share biblical truth. Tell people about Jesus. Serve your church. Care for suffering people. Give generously where God leads you.
Following keeps this kind of biblical encouragement near you.
Sharing carries it beyond you.
Tagging can put it directly in front of someone you love.
Commenting reminds another hurting believer that they are not the only one fighting.
Saving gives you something to return to when the night becomes heavy again.
If you want to support that mission and go deeper with us:
But before you leave, remember the person underneath the broom tree.
Elijah thought he was finished.
God was not finished.
Remember the psalmist talking to his own downcast soul.
“Hope in God.”
Remember Paul, crushed beyond his own strength, learning not to rely upon himself but upon the God who raises the dead.
And above all...
remember Jesus.
Crucified.
Buried.
Risen.
Your darkness is real.
But it is not Lord.
Your feelings are real.
But they are not your Savior.
Your suffering may become part of your story.
But through Jesus Christ, suffering does not have authority to write the ending.
Maybe you came to this article asking:
“Can I be depressed and still trust Jesus?”
Yes.
You can weep and trust Jesus.
You can tremble and trust Jesus.
You can receive treatment and trust Jesus.
You can tell someone you are struggling and trust Jesus.
You can have questions and still bring those questions to Jesus.
You can be exhausted and keep reaching toward Jesus.
Sometimes trust does not look like standing triumphantly above the darkness.
Sometimes trust looks like collapsing into the arms of Christ and discovering that when you could no longer hold onto Him with strength...
He was still holding you.
And perhaps tonight you do not need enough strength to see the entire road ahead.
Perhaps you only need enough strength for one prayer.
“Jesus, keep me.”
And if that is all you have...
give Him that.
Because the Savior who walked out of a sealed tomb is not intimidated by the darkness you cannot yet walk out of.
The night inside you may be louder than your faith right now—but the risen Christ is louder than the grave.
